prompt: Helena tells Davi that Otávio will stop him on the second slide. Which of these are among the four questions an executive brings to a strategy review? Choose all that apply.
hint: Risk, money, time and the decision.

choices.text: What happens if we do nothing?
choices.why: Yes: that is the risk question, answered in money a year.

choices.text: How does the reservation module hold a seat?
choices.why: That is the question Davi's first draft answered, and nobody in the room asked it.

choices.text: What do you need from me today?
choices.why: Yes: the decision, and the row presentations most often leave empty.

choices.text: When do we see the result?
choices.why: Yes: time, answered as a date in the business's calendar.

prompt: Match each technical answer to the answer Otávio can use in its place.

pairs.left: The reservation module is fragile under load
pairs.right: We expect to lose R$ 364,800 a year in failed on-sales
The fix costs R$ 48,000 of engineering time, and nobody new is hired
Before this year's on-sale season, measured by a load test

right_distractors: The module will be rewritten as microservices

prompt: A review ends with everyone agreeing the presentation was clear, and with no decision taken. What does the lesson say about it?
hint: What is different the next morning?

choices.text: It went well, and the decision will follow by e-mail
choices.why: A decision deferred to e-mail is the empty fourth row, with a promise attached.

choices.text: It has not happened
choices.why: Right: nothing is different the next morning, whatever was presented.

choices.text: It was too short for the executives to decide
choices.why: Length is not the problem; the decision wanted was never written down and asked for.

choices.text: It succeeded at informing, which is half the job
choices.why: A review exists to decide. Informing without a decision leaves everything as it was.

prompt: Davi has one proposal: the Reservations team and the fix. Why does the lesson want him to price doing nothing before presenting it?

choices.text: To make the proposal look cheaper by comparison
choices.why: The comparison is honest rather than flattering: doing nothing is a real option with a real price.

choices.text: Finance rules require two options in every request
choices.why: No rule is mentioned. The reason is how executives decide.

choices.text: To show the debt's interest, which Otávio has not seen
choices.why: The interest is part of the do-nothing price, and the reason for pricing it is the comparison, not the novelty.

choices.text: Doing nothing is the one option they always have
choices.why: Right: with one proposal and no priced alternative, the choice is yes or an argument; the do-nothing line is what every proposal is measured against.

prompt: Coreto has 12 big on-sales a year, each with an 8% chance of failing. How many failures does it expect in a year?
A failed on-sale costs Coreto R$ 380,000, and it expects 0.96 failures a year. What is the expected loss a year, in reais?
The season passes and no big on-sale fails. Otávio asks whether the 0.96 was wrong. What is the answer the lesson prepares?

choices.text: Yes, and the estimate should be lowered to zero
choices.why: One year without a failure is what an average of 0.96 predicts for some years; it does not move the estimate to zero.

choices.text: No: it is an average, and some years have none
choices.why: Right: presented as an average, the number survives a year with no failure and a year with two.

choices.text: No: the deploy freeze prevented the failure
choices.why: That may or may not be true, and it does not answer whether 0.96 was a forecast.

choices.text: Yes: it was a forecast of about one failure
choices.why: Reading it as a forecast is the mistake the lesson warns against; a count of failures is a whole number.

prompt: Otávio thinks the 8% is four times too high and the real chance is 2%. What happens to the case for the R$ 48,000 fix?

choices.text: It stands, at about 1.9 times the fix
choices.why: Right: R$ 91,200 against R$ 48,000. The 8% would have to be about 7.6 times too high before the fix stopped paying.

choices.text: It fails: at 2% the fix costs more than the risk
choices.why: At 2% the expected loss is 12 × 2% × R$ 380,000 = R$ 91,200 a year, still above the fix.

choices.text: It depends on the cost of a failure, which also falls
choices.why: The cost of a failure is a separate input, agreed with finance; changing the chance does not change it.

choices.text: Nobody can say until the 8% is measured again
choices.why: The point of the break-even is that the decision does not wait for a better estimate: anything above about 1% keeps it.

prompt: Which title passes the lesson's test for a strategy slide?
hint: If only the title survived, could Otávio say yes or no to it?

choices.text: Reservation module: current state and proposal
choices.why: It names a topic and asks for nothing; it is Davi's first title.

choices.text: Seat holds are the main cause of on-sale failures
choices.why: A full sentence and true, and it still asks for no decision.

choices.text: Fix the seat holds first: R$ 48,000 once, R$ 364,800 a year
choices.why: Right: it says what to do, by when, and the two numbers that justify it.

choices.text: Protecting the on-sale: our technical strategy for the coming year
choices.why: It sounds like a decision and is a heading: there is nothing in it to approve.

prompt: Put the parts of Davi's slide in the order a reader meets them, from the top.
hint: The claim first; the caveat last.
items: The title, stating the decision and its two numbers
What is going on, and the money, side by side
The decision we need today, and what waits a year
The footer: how we will know, and the caveat
trap: Putting the decision last is the deck habit the lesson replaces: the reader reaches the ask after the attention has gone.

prompt: Why does the slide have a box for what waits a year?
hint: The half of the decision people forget.

choices.text: To reassure the two team leads that their projects are not cancelled
choices.why: The leads were told in person. The box is for the people approving the decision.

choices.text: Approving the team is also approving that two projects wait
choices.why: Right: a box makes it a choice taken with open eyes, instead of a surprise later.

choices.text: To fill the layout's fourth box
choices.why: The layout has the box because of what it holds, not the other way round.

choices.text: Finance needs the list to move those budgets
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson is about moving budgets; the box is about seeing the whole decision.

prompt: The decision box ends with "No new hires." What does that sentence do for Otávio?
hint: How does a CFO read "a team of four"?

choices.text: It shows the team costs Coreto nothing at all
choices.why: The team costs what its engineers stop doing; the sentence says what it does not cost, which is new salaries.

choices.text: It is a promise to the two team leads
choices.why: The slide's reader is the CFO; the leads are told in person.

choices.text: It answers his first question before he asks it
choices.why: Right: he reads "a team of four" as four salaries until told otherwise; the real cost is the work those four stop doing, lesson 13's opportunity cost.

choices.text: It replaces the money box for this particular reader
choices.why: The money box carries the risk against the fix; this sentence heads off a different misreading.

prompt: Match each question from the review to the lesson whose work answered it.

pairs.left: What do we pay if we wait?
Why buy search instead of building?
Aren't we locked in to the gateway?
Why the fix before Pix in instalments?

prompt: Davi reads the slide's title aloud and stops talking. Why does the lesson call that pause deliberate?
hint: What is the meeting made of?

choices.text: To give the executives time to read the four boxes
choices.why: Reading is part of it, but the point is what comes after: the questions.

choices.text: Silence pressures the CFO into approving quickly
choices.why: The lesson wants the strategy pushed on, not rushed through.

choices.text: Helena asked him to keep it short
choices.why: Helena's advice was to start with cost; the pause is Davi's own design.

choices.text: The questions are the meeting, and they test the strategy
choices.why: Right: filling the hour with the appendix protects the strategy from the only test that matters.

prompt: Helena asks: "What would make you change this?" What kind of answer does Davi give?

choices.text: Conditions somebody could check
choices.why: Right: a load-test result and a count of failed on-sales, each of which would send the strategy back to the room.

choices.text: That nothing would, because the numbers are clear
choices.why: A strategy that admits nothing could change it gets changed by whoever asks loudest instead.

choices.text: A new CFO or CTO with different priorities
choices.why: That is a change of people, not a reason; the lesson wants evidence that would change the diagnosis.

choices.text: A competitor shipping microservices first
choices.why: Nothing in Coreto's diagnosis depends on competitors' architecture.

prompt: Otávio asks what a 10% cut would mean. Why is Davi's answer — 6.6 engineers, or 68% of the cloud bill — more useful than "R$ 1,738,400" alone?

choices.text: It shows that a cut of that size is impossible to make
choices.why: The cut is possible; the answer shows what it would actually remove.

choices.text: It shows what the cut would remove: mostly people
choices.why: Right: a percentage of a budget that is 79.0% people becomes a number of engineers, and the cloud comparison shows no other line is big enough.

choices.text: Reais impress a CFO less than a count of people does
choices.why: A CFO thinks in reais. The point is translating a share into its consequence.

choices.text: It avoids the question by switching to other units
choices.why: It answers the question in reais first and then says what those reais are.

prompt: The expected loss is R$ 364,800 a year and the fix costs R$ 48,000 once. How many times the fix is one year of expected loss? Give one decimal place.
The expected loss of R$ 364,800 is an ___ over many years, not a forecast for this one.
A colleague suggests one line on the slide: R$ 120,900 of interest plus R$ 364,800 of expected loss, R$ 485,700 a year. What does the lesson say?
hint: Which of the two is cash?

choices.text: Use it: the bigger number makes the case stronger
choices.why: A bigger number built from two kinds of money is weaker, because it invites the whole total to be discounted.

choices.text: Drop the interest, since it is already paid
choices.why: The interest is real: engineers' time spent working around the module. It belongs on its own line.

choices.text: Keep two lines: they are different money
choices.why: Right: the first person in finance to notice the mix discounts the total, and each line alone already justifies the fix.

choices.text: Use it, but round it to half a million
choices.why: Rounding does not fix mixing salary time with revenue, and it adds a number nobody computed.

prompt: Rafaela, the Platform lead, wants Otávio to approve a year of work on the golden-path templates. Her draft opens with how the templates generate a new service. By the lesson, what should open it instead?

choices.text: A simplified diagram of the template, so he understands it
choices.why: A simplified mechanism is still a mechanism: too technical for the CFO and too vague for the CTO.

choices.text: A history of how Platform came to own the templates
choices.why: That is the deck that walks through the work in the order it was done, and reaches the ask last.

choices.text: The adoption figures, because they are her best evidence
choices.why: Evidence belongs under the claim. Without a stated decision, good evidence supports nothing in particular.

choices.text: The decision she wants from him, with its cost and its date
choices.why: Right: a verb, an owner and a date in the title, and the money beneath it, as the four questions ask.
